data.title: Reorder List
data.summary:
Input: A singly linked list head.
Output: The list modified in-place such that nodes are reordered from L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ...
Rules: Do not change the values in the nodes; only the node pointers can be modified.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 5 * 10^4].

data.reference_solution:
def reorderList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return
    nodes = []
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nodes.append(curr)
        curr = curr.next
    i, j = 0, len(nodes) - 1
    while i < j:
        nodes[i].next = nodes[j]
        i += 1
        if i == j:
            break
        nodes[j].next = nodes[i]
        j -= 1
    nodes[i].next = None
data.checker_code:
def check(args, got, expected):
    head = args[0]
    vals = []
    curr = head
    seen = set()
    while curr:
        if id(curr) in seen:
            return False
        seen.add(id(curr))
        vals.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    
    n = len(vals)
    expected_vals = []
    i, j = 0, n - 1
    while i <= j:
        if i == j:
            expected_vals.append(vals[i])
        else:
            expected_vals.append(vals[i])
            expected_vals.append(vals[j])
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    
    orig_head = args[0]
    curr = orig_head
    for v in expected_vals:
        if not curr or curr.val != v:
            return False
        curr = curr.next
    if curr is not None:
        return False
    return True

data.approach: Find middle, reverse second half, and merge
data.key_insight: A linked list reordering like L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 can be achieved by splitting the list into two halves, reversing the second half, and then alternately merging the nodes from both halves.

steps.title: Find the middle of the linked list
steps.detail: Use the fast and slow pointer technique to find the middle node, which splits the list into two halves.

steps.title: Reverse the second half
steps.detail: Reverse the linked list starting from the node immediately after the middle node to properly order elements for the merge.

steps.title: Merge the two halves
steps.detail: Interleave nodes from the first half and the reversed second half in place to produce the final reordered list.

data.code:
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        if not head or not head.next:
            return
        
        slow = fast = head
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        
        prev = None
        curr = slow.next
        slow.next = None
        while curr:
            next_temp = curr.next
            curr.next = prev
            prev = curr
            curr = next_temp
        
        first = head
        second = prev
        while second:
            tmp1, tmp2 = first.next, second.next
            first.next = second
            second.next = tmp1
            first, second = tmp1, tmp2

data.pattern_summary: Two pointers involve maintaining indices or references that move through the data structure in a coordinated way, often from opposite ends or at different speeds, to process elements efficiently.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Using pointers from the start and end of the list allows you to weave the nodes together directly.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: A hash map stores value-to-index mappings, but does not help structure pointer reassignments for sequence interleaving.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Sliding windows deal with contiguous subarrays or sublists of a fixed size, not alternating endpoints across the entire structure.

pattern_options.name: Depth-first search
pattern_options.feedback: DFS explores tree or graph structures along branches, whereas a linked list reorder requires linear structural manipulation.

signals.phrase: reordered from L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2
signals.hint: This alternating pattern from both extremities points toward using pointers at opposite ends of the structure.

signals.phrase: only the node pointers can be modified
signals.hint: You must physically rearrange connections rather than copying data into a separate array and modifying values.

data.brute_force_idea: Store all node references in a Python list, then use two indices starting at opposite ends to reassign the .next pointers inward until they meet in the middle.
data.brute_force_why: Traversing the list takes O(n) time, and iterating through the array of nodes with two pointers also takes O(n) operations.
data.bottleneck: The straightforward array-based approach already runs in O(n) time, meaning every node is visited a constant number of times. There is no wasted work or redundant traversal to remove.
bottleneck_hints: Consider how many times you must traverse the linked list to find its elements.
Look at the time complexity of collecting all nodes into an array versus the traversal steps.
Recognize that visiting every node at least once is a fundamental requirement to rewire the pointers.

data.insight: The brute force solution requires O(n) extra space to store all node references in an array for indexing. The optimized solution eliminates this memory overhead by breaking the list into two halves, reversing the second half in place, and interleaving them. We use the slow and fast pointer technique to find the middle without extra storage.

derivation.note: The fast pointer traverses the list two steps at a time, finding the middle.
The second half of the list is reversed node by node.
The first and reversed second halves are merged together.

data.time_summary: Lines 7, 14, and 22 each run in proportional to n/2 steps. Adding these linear passes together results in O(n) total time, which matches the measured step growth from 26 to 208 as n scales from 4 to 32.
data.space_summary: O(1) extra space because we only reassign existing node pointers and do not allocate any new data structures like arrays or hash maps.
data.takeaway: When asked to rearrange a linked list in a non-standard order without extra memory, split the list into halves, reverse the relevant portion, and merge them back together.
mistakes: Forgetting to sever the connection between the first half and the second half at slow.next = None, which leaves a cycle in the linked list.
Losing track of node references during the in-place reversal or merge phase by updating pointers in the wrong order.
Failing to handle edge cases where the linked list has fewer than three nodes.

data.overview: The algorithm reorders a singly linked list in-place by splitting it into two halves, reversing the second half, and alternately merging the nodes from both halves together.
data.intuition: Imagine cutting a deck of cards in half, flipping the bottom half upside down, and then interleaving the cards one by one from the top and bottom piles.
